snip.t: Hypertension: Left ventricular hypertrophy, atrial stretch — Very common, major risk factor for AF.
Cardiovascular Disease: Accelerated atherosclerosis, hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias.
Left ventricular hypertrophy and coronary blood flow inadequate to suppy the myocardium – angina

In acute severe regurgitation (e.g. perforation of aortic cusp in endocarditis), there may be no time for compensatory left ventricular hypertrophy and dilatation to develop and the features of heart failure may predominate.

qs.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic hypertension presents with dyspnea on exertion and normal ejection fraction. Echocardiography shows marked left ventricular hypertrophy and normal chamber size. Which underlying pathophysiological process is primarily responsible for her symptoms?
o: Inability to achieve adequate systolic contraction
Abnormal regurgitant flow across heart valves
qs.e: Diastolic dysfunction is characterized by impaired ventricular relaxation and reduced compliance, leading to elevated filling pressures with a preserved ejection fraction. Systolic dysfunction instead refers to the inability of the heart to generate adequate forward flow through contraction.

qs.q: What is the primary histological feature observed in cardiomyocytes of a patient with systemic hypertensive heart disease causing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy?
qs.e: Hypertensive heart disease leads to enlarged cardiomyocytes with large nuclei, known as boxcar nuclei, along with interstitial fibrosis. Coagulative necrosis and neutrophil infiltration are acute changes seen in myocardial infarction.

qs.q: A 65-year-old man with aortic stenosis develops left ventricular hypertrophy. This adaptation will eventually fail primarily because:
o: Myocytes reach maximum size and cannot enlarge further
Blood supply cannot keep pace with increased metabolic demands
Sarcomeres become disorganized with further stress
qs.e: Cardiac hypertrophy increases metabolic demands of the enlarged myocytes. When blood supply cannot match these demands (relative ischemia), the adaptation fails and progresses to heart failure. While apoptosis may occur later and sarcomere disorganization happens, the primary reason for failure is inadequate perfusion of the hypertrophied muscle mass creating an energy deficit.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is the thickening of the left ventricular wall due to chronic pressure or volume overload. It alters myocardial structure, reduces compliance, and predisposes to arrhythmias and heart failure.

sections.p: LVH is defined by increased left ventricular mass or wall thickness on imaging or ECG. Diagnosis combines clinical context, imaging, and ECG criteria.
b: Increased LV mass >115 g/m² (men) or >95 g/m² (women) on echo or MRI

t.b: Measures wall thickness and mass; a value above normal indicates LVH and helps stage severity.
Detects voltage criteria for LVH; positive findings support but are less sensitive than imaging.
Gold standard for mass measurement; used when echo is inconclusive or for precise staging.

sections.p: LVH is staged by wall thickness and mass, correlating with risk of complications.

t.b: Determines stage; higher thickness predicts arrhythmia risk.

sections.p: The most common drivers are chronic pressure overload from hypertension and aortic stenosis, followed by volume overload from valvular regurgitation.

t.b: Elevated systolic pressure indicates pressure overload; treat to reduce LVH.
Identifies valvular lesions causing volume or pressure overload.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with exertional dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.

t.b: Detects arrhythmias; presence of atrial fibrillation or ventricular ectopy suggests advanced LVH.

sections.p: Investigations confirm LVH, assess cause, and evaluate complications.

t.b: Measures wall thickness, mass, and valve function; identifies cause and severity.
Shows voltage criteria and arrhythmia patterns; helps rule out other causes.
Elevated levels indicate myocardial strain and risk of heart failure.
May show cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion.
Assesses comorbidities that can worsen LVH or mask symptoms.

sections.p: LVH can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and ischemia.

t.b: Reduced relaxation predicts heart failure risk.
Detects ventricular ectopy; frequent ectopy raises sudden death risk.

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, control blood pressure, and use drugs that reduce afterload and improve diastolic function.
b: Lifestyle: salt restriction, weight control, exercise

t.b: Reduces afterload, slows LVH regression, and improves survival.
Controls heart rate, reduces myocardial oxygen demand, and prevents arrhythmias.
Relieves congestion in heart failure; avoid if renal function is poor.
Used if dyslipidemia present; reduces atherosclerotic risk.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood pressure, ECG, and echocardiography is essential to track regression and detect complications.

t.b: Maintaining target BP slows LVH progression.
Detects new arrhythmias early.

sections.p: LVH can be mistaken for left ventricular dilation or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
ECG voltage criteria may be normal in obese patients or high in athletes; imaging is needed for confirmation.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of LVH?
faq.a: Hypertension is the leading cause worldwide.
